artworks.title: Acheulean hand axe, Saint-Acheul

location.name: Chapel Hill, North Carolina
location.institution: Research Laboratories of Archaeology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (North Carolina Archaeological Collection)

artworks.medium: Bifacially knapped flint
artworks.description: The hand axe is the signature tool of the Acheulean, a tradition that early humans sustained for well over a million years across Africa, Europe and Asia. Each one was shaped by striking flakes from both faces of a flint nodule until a symmetrical, teardrop cutting edge remained. This example comes from the gravel pits of Saint-Acheul at Amiens, the site that gave the industry its name, and still bears its 1920s collector's label.
facts: The Acheulean is named after Saint-Acheul, a suburb of Amiens, where hand axes were found in the Somme river gravels in the 19th century.
Hand axes were made from roughly 1.6 million to about 100,000 years ago, chiefly by Homo erectus and its successors, and only rarely by Homo sapiens.
Jacques Boucher de Perthes's finds in the Somme gravels in the 1840s helped establish that humans had coexisted with extinct Ice Age animals.

credit.author: Research Laboratories of Archaeology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (model by Kay Waller)

contributed.note: Photogrammetry scan of a real flint hand axe, catalogue 516a5, published CC0 by UNC's Research Laboratories of Archaeology on Sketchfab (https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/acheulean-hand-axe-516a5-ab5a9c0862974e2b99a951ac4776257e, uid ab5a9c0862974e2b99a951ac4776257e, user rla-archaeology) and mirrored as a glb on Zenodo ('Source: Objaverse 1.0 / Sketchfab', DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21530762); anonymous download verified. The RLA description gives the findspot as 'Montieres Amiens, France'; the old collector's ink label visible on the scan reads 'AMIENS - ST. ACHEUL ... Ach. 516A5', i.e. the Acheulean type site (Montières and Saint-Acheul are quarters of Amiens). Raw glb: 60,000 triangles, one texture, bounding box 2.6514 x 1.0572 x 1.5256 units; real length 99.3 mm, so scale = 0.0993/2.6514 = 0.03745 m per unit. Use the raw '<uid>.glb', not the '_normalized' variants. Dimensions (99.3 x 60.6 x 31.4 mm), material and 'Lower Paleolithic (before 300,000 years ago)' from the RLA description; the broader Acheulean range (c. 1.6 million to 100,000 years ago) from Wikipedia 'Hand axe'. Collected 1929 by James Bell Bullitt, donated to UNC. No Smithsonian/Met scan found.

artworks.title: Löwenmensch (Lion-man) of Hohlenstein-Stadel
artworks.medium: Carved mammoth ivory
artworks.description: A standing figure with a human body and the head of a cave lion, carved from a mammoth tusk with flint tools. Found in fragments in the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in the Swabian Jura in 1939, it was reassembled over decades from more than two hundred pieces and is among the oldest known figurative sculptures.
facts: Discovered on 25 August 1939 by Otto Völzing, a week before the Second World War halted the dig.
Radiocarbon dating of its find layer places it between 35,000 and 41,000 years old.
Seven parallel transverse gouges are carved into the left arm; the 2012-13 restoration raised its height from 29.6 to 31.1 cm.

contributed.note: Original figurine photographed in Museum Ulm, frontal three-quarter view on a plain dark background; this is also the English Wikipedia infobox image. File metadata from the Commons imageinfo API. Object data: Dates: Wikipedia (35,000-41,000 years old; Wikidata inception c. 38,000 BCE). Dimensions 31.1 x 5.6 x 5.9 cm: Wikipedia lead. Find-spot coordinates: Wikidata Q1498134 (Hohlenstein-Stadel). Discovery date: Wikipedia/Wikidata. Museum Ulm inventory number not published on Wikipedia/Wikidata.

artworks.title: Hand stencils, Leang Pettakere
artworks.medium: red ochre sprayed over the hand
artworks.description: Hands held against the limestone and sprayed with red ochre, in one of the Maros-Pangkep karst caves of southern Sulawesi. A stencil in the neighbouring cave of Leang Timpuseng is at least 39,900 years old, which made the Sulawesi caves the oldest dated figurative rock art in the world when it was published in 2014, older than anything then dated in Europe.
facts: The age comes from uranium-series dating of the calcite 'cave popcorn' that grew over the paintings, which gives a minimum age.
A nearby painting of a Sulawesi warty pig at Leang Tedongnge was later dated to at least 45,500 years.
The stencils are negative images: the hand is the unpainted part.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of the cave wall

artworks.title: Panel of the Lions, Chauvet Cave

location.name: Vallon-Pont-d'Arc
location.institution: Grotte Chauvet (sealed; shown from the Grotte Chauvet 2 facsimile)

artworks.medium: charcoal and scraping on limestone
artworks.description: The right part of the Panel of the Lions in the deepest chamber of Chauvet Cave: a pride of lions, drawn without manes, stalks a herd of bison. The charcoal was drawn on a wall first scraped clean, and the artists shaded with their fingers to round the bodies. This photograph is of the full-scale facsimile at Grotte Chauvet 2, since the cave itself has been closed to the public since its discovery in 1994.
facts: Chauvet's oldest drawings are around 36,000 years old, twice the age of Lascaux.
A rockfall sealed the cave about 21,000 years ago, which is why the drawings survive so well.
Werner Herzog filmed the panels in 3D for Cave of Forgotten Dreams (2010).

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of the Grotte Chauvet 2 facsimile

artworks.title: Venus of Willendorf

madeIn.name: Willendorf II site, Willendorf in der Wachau

artworks.medium: Carved oolitic limestone with traces of red ochre
artworks.description: A palm-sized female figure with exaggerated breasts, belly and hips, a patterned head without a face, and no feet. It was carved from an oolitic limestone not found locally and once tinted with red ochre. Found in 1908 in loess deposits beside the Danube at Willendorf, it is the best-known of the Palaeolithic Venus figurines.
facts: Recovered on 7 August 1908 during a dig led by Josef Szombathy, Hugo Obermaier and Josef Bayer.
Radiocarbon dates from the surrounding layers suggest it was buried about 30,000 years ago.
Its limestone is not local to the Wachau; the name Venus is a modern label, and some scholars prefer Woman of Willendorf.

contributed.note: Original figurine at the Naturhistorisches Museum Wien, frontal view on a black background. CC BY (no share-alike). File metadata from the Commons imageinfo API. Object data: Date c. 30,000 BP: Wikipedia infobox; yearStart/yearEnd span the Gravettian range Wikipedia gives (33,000-20,000 years ago). Height 11.1 cm: Wikipedia lead and Wikidata P2048; width/depth not given there. Find-spot coordinates: Wikidata Q9374772 (Willendorf II). NHM inventory number not given on Wikipedia/Wikidata.

artworks.title: Megaloceros, Lascaux

location.name: Montignac-Lascaux
location.institution: Grotte de Lascaux (sealed; replica photographed at the Anthropos museum, Brno)

artworks.medium: mineral pigment on limestone
artworks.description: A giant deer with its enormous antlers thrown back, painted in black manganese with a red ochre ground and a line of black dots beneath. It stands near the end of the Axial Gallery of Lascaux, among the horses and aurochs that made the cave famous after four teenagers found it in 1940. The cave was closed in 1963 because visitors' breath was growing algae and calcite over the paintings; this is a museum replica.
facts: Megaloceros giganteus, the Irish elk, carried antlers up to 3.6 metres across and died out about 7,700 years ago.
Lascaux holds about 600 painted animals and nearly 1,500 engravings.
The dots and squares scattered around the animals have never been decoded.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of a museum replica, released to the public domain by the photographer

artworks.title: Polychrome ceiling, Altamira

location.name: Santillana del Mar
location.institution: Cueva de Altamira (closed; reproduction photographed at the Deutsches Museum, Munich)

artworks.medium: ochre and charcoal on limestone
artworks.description: The great ceiling of Altamira, where a herd of bison is painted in red ochre and outlined in black over the natural bulges of the rock, so that each animal stands out as if in relief. Found in 1879 by Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola and his young daughter María, it was the first Palaeolithic cave art recognised as such, after two decades of scholars dismissing it as a forgery. The cave is closed to protect the paintings; this is the full-size reproduction in Munich.
facts: The polychrome bison date to around 14,500 years ago; the oldest marks in the cave are over 35,000 years old.
The ceiling is about 18 metres long and was painted lying down, under a roof little more than a metre high.
Picasso is often quoted as saying that after Altamira, all is decadence.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of the Deutsches Museum reproduction

artworks.title: Clovis point (Clovis lanceolate spear point)

location.name: Chapel Hill, North Carolina
location.institution: Research Laboratories of Archaeology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (North Carolina Archaeological Collection)

artworks.medium: Knapped metavolcanic stone, fluted lanceolate projectile point
artworks.description: Clovis points are the fluted, lance-shaped spear tips of the Clovis culture, the earliest widespread tool tradition in the Americas. A shallow channel, or flute, struck from the base on each face let the point be seated in a split wooden or bone shaft. This example, knapped from metavolcanic stone, was found in the Piedmont of North Carolina and donated to the University of North Carolina, whose archaeology laboratory made the scan.
facts: Clovis points are named after Clovis, New Mexico, where the first examples were found in 1929 by Ridgely Whiteman.
All known Clovis points date to roughly 13,400–12,700 years ago, often in association with mammoth and other Ice Age animal remains.
Finished points were fluted on both faces so they could be hafted; the technique was passed between knappers across the continent.

credit.author: Research Laboratories of Archaeology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (model by Steve Davis)

contributed.note: Photogrammetry scan of a real Clovis point, published CC0 by UNC's Research Laboratories of Archaeology on Sketchfab (https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/clovis-lanceolate-f5a48834fc66497ebc416ef94ec2eeeb, uid f5a48834fc66497ebc416ef94ec2eeeb, user rla-archaeology) and mirrored as a glb on Zenodo ('Source: Objaverse 1.0 / Sketchfab', DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21490444), which downloads anonymously (verified HTTP 200, 3.1 MB). Raw Sketchfab-export glb: 87,188 triangles, one texture, no Draco; bounding box 2.5213 x 0.216 x 0.9737 units. Real length 84.5 mm (RLA description), so scale = 0.0845/2.5213 = 0.0335 m per unit; drop into data/originals/<id>/ with provenance 'sketchfab' and set scale accordingly. The record also carries '_normalized' variants (unit-cube rescaled) which should NOT be used. Dimensions (84.5 x 32.8 x 6.7 mm) and findspot from the RLA description; date range from Wikipedia 'Clovis point' (13,400-12,700 years ago). No Smithsonian or Met scan of a Clovis point was found (3d.si.edu blocked scripted access; the Smithsonian's Sketchfab mirror has none).

artworks.title: Nordeste tradition figures, Serra da Capivara

creators.name: Unknown painters of the Nordeste tradition

artworks.medium: red ochre on sandstone
artworks.description: A red deer-like animal and small human figures on a sandstone shelter in the Serra da Capivara, where more than a thousand painted shelters record hunting, dancing and sex in the lively Nordeste style. The park is at the centre of the argument over when people reached the Americas: its excavator Niède Guidon claims hearths over 30,000 years old, far older than most archaeologists accept.
facts: Serra da Capivara holds the largest concentration of rock art in the Americas.
The Nordeste tradition is usually dated between about 12,000 and 6,000 years ago.
Capivara means capybara, the park's name animal.

externalIds.commons-file: Pintura rupestre no Parque Nacional Serra da Capivara (0356).jpg

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of the shelter wall

artworks.title: Rock Shelter 8, Bhimbetka

creators.name: Unknown Mesolithic painters of central India

artworks.medium: ochre on sandstone
artworks.description: A frieze of red animals and small hunters inside one of the sandstone shelters at Bhimbetka, south of Bhopal, where some 750 shelters were painted over and over from the Mesolithic to the medieval period. The oldest figures, like these, are red; later ones are white and show riders, elephants and battles.
facts: The shelters were noticed by the archaeologist V. S. Wakankar from a train window in 1957.
Stone tools in the shelters go back 100,000 years, long before the paintings.
Bhimbetka was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2003.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of the shelter wall

artworks.title: Cueva de las Manos
artworks.medium: mineral pigment blown through bone pipes
artworks.description: Hundreds of hands stencilled in red, white, black and ochre on the wall of a cave above the Río Pinturas in Patagonia. The painters held a hand to the rock and blew pigment over it through a bone pipe; most are left hands, so the pipe was held in the right. Guanaco hunts and geometric patterns were painted around them over several thousand years.
facts: The oldest layer has been dated to around 9,300 years ago.
Of about 830 hands, only 31 are right hands.
The cave was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1999.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph released to the public domain by the photographer

artworks.title: Pastoral figures, Tanzoumaitak, Tassili n'Ajjer

creators.name: Unknown painters of the Saharan Pastoral period

artworks.medium: ochre on sandstone
artworks.description: Running and dancing figures in ochre on a sandstone shelter at Tanzoumaitak, on the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau in the Algerian Sahara. When they were painted the Sahara was green: the plateau's 15,000 paintings and engravings show cattle herds, giraffes, hippos and swimmers where there is now only rock and sand.
facts: Henri Lhote's expeditions in the 1950s, guided by the Tuareg Jebrine ag Mohamed, copied thousands of the paintings and made the site famous.
The Round Head period, the plateau's oldest painted style, may go back 10,000 years; the Pastoral period that follows is the richest.
Tassili n'Ajjer was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1982.

externalIds.commons-file: The Tanzoumaitak cave painting in Tassili n'ajjer.jpg

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of the shelter wall

artworks.title: Cattle, Laas Geel

creators.name: Unknown Neolithic painters of the Horn of Africa

artworks.medium: ochre, white and black pigment on granite
artworks.description: Long-horned cows with decorated necks and ceremonial collars, painted in red, white and black on the ceiling of a granite shelter at Laas Geel, outside Hargeisa. The cows are shown with their udders and without legs below the knee, as if seen from the front, and small human figures stand beneath them with their arms raised. The site is among the best preserved rock art in Africa.
facts: Local herders had always known the shelters; a French team recorded them for archaeology in 2002.
There are about twenty painted shelters on the granite outcrop.
Laas Geel means 'the camels' waterhole' in Somali.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of the shelter ceiling

artworks.title: Proto-cuneiform tablet: account of barley distribution

madeIn.name: Southern Mesopotamia (find-spot unrecorded; placed at Uruk)

location.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

artworks.medium: Clay, impressed with a stylus and a cylinder seal
artworks.description: A small clay tablet recording the distribution of barley in the pictographic proto-cuneiform script, the earliest stage of writing in Mesopotamia. Numerical notations are pressed into the clay with the round end of a stylus beside signs for the commodity and its recipients. The reverse and edges were rolled with a cylinder seal showing a man with hunting dogs and boars.
facts: Dated by the Met to about 3100-2900 BCE, the Jemdet Nasr period, when writing was still largely pictographic.
The tablet measures 5.4 by 6 by 4.1 cm and entered the Met in 1988 as a Raymond and Beverly Sackler gift purchase.
Proto-cuneiform tablets are almost all administrative records, listing goods, rations and labour rather than language as speech.

externalIds.commons-file: Cuneiform tablet- administrative account of barley distribution with cylinder seal impression of a male figure, hunting dogs, and boars MET DT847.jpg

credit.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

contributed.note: Met studio photograph of the obverse on a plain grey ground, donated to Commons under CC0 as part of the Met Open Access programme. Met object 329081, accession 1988.433.1; the Met's current primary image is https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/an/original/DP293243.jpg (also CC0). Dates, dimensions and period from the Met collection API. Object data: All object data from the Met collection API object 329081 (date ca. 3100-2900 BCE, Jemdet Nasr period, Sumerian, clay, 5.4 x 6 x 4.1 cm, accession 1988.433.1, credit line 'Purchase, Raymond and Beverly Sackler Gift, 1988'). The Met records only 'Mesopotamia' as geography, so no find-spot coordinates are given; if a geo position is required, Uruk (Wikidata Q168518, 31.3259, 45.6374), the main source of proto-cuneiform tablets, is a defensible approximation but should be labelled as such.

artworks.title: Nebra sky disc
artworks.medium: Bronze disc with gold inlays
artworks.description: A bronze disc with a blue-green patina inlaid with gold symbols: a full sun or moon, a crescent, a cluster of seven stars read as the Pleiades, two horizon arcs marking the solstice sunrise and sunset, and a boat. Buried on the Mittelberg near Nebra with swords, axes and arm spirals, it is the oldest known concrete depiction of the night sky.
facts: Found in 1999 by two unlicensed metal-detectorists and recovered by police in a sting in Basel in 2002.
About 30 cm across and 2.2 kg; 38 to 40 holes were punched around the rim before burial.
Added to the UNESCO Memory of the World Register in 2013.

externalIds.commons-file: Himmelsscheibe von Nebra - Landesmuseum für Vorgeschichte in Halle - HD.jpg

contributed.note: Original disc photographed in its permanent display at the Landesmuseum für Vorgeschichte, Halle, square frontal view on a dark ground; 39 MB original, so fetch via Commons thumbnail widths. The widely used 'Nebra disc 1.jpg' (Frank Vincentz, PD) was taken at the Gasometer Oberhausen 'Der schöne Schein' show, which exhibited replicas, so it is avoided. File metadata from the Commons imageinfo API. Object data: Date c. 1800-1600 BCE, culture, diameter about 30 cm and weight 2.2 kg: Wikipedia lead and infobox (citing the Halle museum). Wikidata Q157094 instead gives 32 cm and 2,050 g; the museum's own page could not be scraped for numbers. Find-spot coordinates 51.28389, 11.52 (Mittelberg): Wikipedia infobox coord and Wikidata P625. Halle inventory number not published on Wikipedia/Wikidata.

artworks.title: Neck-amphora with a wedding procession, by Exekias

location.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
location.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

artworks.medium: Terracotta, black-figure
artworks.description: Lidded neck-amphora attributed to Exekias, the leading Athenian black-figure potter-painter of the mid sixth century BC. On the body a couple ride in a four-horse chariot in a procession, accompanied by a kithara player and a foot soldier, beneath a band of palmettes and lotus on the neck. Exekias' work is marked by precise incision and dignified, static compositions; the lid with its bud-shaped knob survives with the vase.
facts: Exekias was active in Athens between roughly 545 and 530 BC and worked as both potter and painter.
The vase stands 47 cm high and 24.8 cm in diameter and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (Rogers Fund, 1917).
Black-figure decoration is painted in a clay slip that fires black, with details incised through to the red clay.

externalIds.commons-file: Terracotta neck-amphora (jar) with lid and knob (27.16) MET DP218568.jpg

credit.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access photograph DP218568)

contributed.note: Met Open Access studio photograph, donated to Commons by the Met; same file served by the Met at https://images.metmuseum.org/CRDImages/gr/original/DP218568.jpg (object 250551). Clean frontal view on a plain grey ground, lid in place. Date, dimensions, accession and culture from the Met collection API (object 250551); creator attribution and depicted subjects from Wikidata Q29383807; Exekias' active dates from en.wikipedia 'Exekias'. The Met page itself returned HTTP 429 during sourcing, so the curatorial text was not read.

artworks.title: Rosetta Stone

madeIn.name: Fort Julien near Rashid (Rosetta), Nile Delta

artworks.medium: Granodiorite stele, incised
artworks.description: A broken granodiorite stele carrying a priestly decree issued at Memphis in 196 BCE for the young king Ptolemy V, written three times: in Egyptian hieroglyphs, in Demotic and in Greek. Found by French soldiers in 1799 built into Fort Julien at Rashid, it passed to Britain in 1801 and gave scholars the key to reading Egyptian hieroglyphs.
facts: Found in July 1799 by Pierre-François Bouchard during the French campaign in Egypt and ceded to Britain under the Capitulation of Alexandria in 1801.
Measures 112.3 by 75.7 by 28.4 cm and weighs about 760 kg; the stone is granodiorite, not basalt as long assumed.
Jean-François Champollion announced the decipherment of the Egyptian scripts in 1822, building on Thomas Young's work.

contributed.note: Original stele in the British Museum, frontal view with the background cut to black; all three scripts legible, no visitors or glass reflections. Wikipedia infobox image. File metadata from the Commons imageinfo API. Object data: Date 196 BCE, dimensions 112.3 x 75.7 x 28.4 cm and weight c. 760 kg: Wikipedia Description section (citing the British Museum) and Wikidata. Inventory EA24: Wikidata P217. Find-spot: Fort Julien, Wikidata Q3077898 coordinates; the stele was probably originally set up in a temple, possibly at Sais, per Wikipedia, so madeIn records the find-spot.

artworks.title: Alexander Mosaic (Battle of Issus)
artworks.movement: Hellenistic mosaic (Roman copy after a Hellenistic painting)
artworks.medium: Floor mosaic, opus vermiculatum
artworks.description: Roman floor mosaic from the House of the Faun at Pompeii, usually dated to about 120–100 BC and thought to copy a lost Hellenistic painting, perhaps by Philoxenus of Eretria. It shows Alexander the Great, bare-headed at the left, charging the Persian king Darius III, who turns in his chariot as his army breaks. Excavated in 1831 and moved to Naples in 1843, it is among the most detailed battle scenes to survive from antiquity.
facts: Discovered in 1831 in the House of the Faun, Pompeii, and transferred to Naples in September 1843.
Made of roughly one to one and a half million tesserae about 2 mm wide, laid in curving opus vermiculatum.
The scene depicts more than fifty figures; it is traditionally identified as the Battle of Issus (333 BC).

credit.author: Unknown Roman mosaicist; reproduction credited to 'art database' (PD-Art)

contributed.note: Flat frontal reproduction of the whole mosaic cropped to its border, 6000 px wide; licensed on Commons as public domain (PD-Art reproduction of a PD 2D work). Date and subject from en.wikipedia 'Alexander Mosaic'; dimensions 582 x 313 cm from it.wikipedia 'Battaglia di Isso (mosaico)' and de.wikipedia 'Alexandermosaik' (Wikidata Q841762 gives width 513 cm, which disagrees; the two Wikipedias agree on 582). Place of making: made for the floor of the House of the Faun, Pompeii (coordinates of the house from Wikidata Q1547308). Inventory number not verified, left null.

artworks.title: The Great Gallery, Horseshoe Canyon

creators.name: Unknown painters of the Barrier Canyon style

artworks.medium: mineral pigment on sandstone
artworks.description: A line of tall, armless, hollow-eyed figures painted in dark red along sixty metres of a sandstone alcove in Horseshoe Canyon, Utah. The Great Gallery is the finest panel of the Barrier Canyon style, named after this canyon; its largest figure, the Holy Ghost, stands over two metres tall and was painted by spraying pigment, with smaller animals and figures around it.
facts: Geologists dated the panel in 2014 by the age of the rockfall it was painted on and the sediment that later buried its base: between about 1 and 1100 CE.
The full panel is about 61 metres long and 4.6 metres high.
Horseshoe Canyon was renamed from Barrier Canyon, but the style kept the old name.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of a section of the panel

artworks.title: X-ray turtle, Kakadu
artworks.medium: ochre on sandstone
artworks.description: A long-necked turtle painted in the X-ray style of western Arnhem Land, with its backbone and organs drawn inside the outline. The X-ray convention appears in Kakadu's galleries over the last two or three thousand years, at the end of a painting tradition that goes back more than 20,000 years, and shows the food animals of the wetlands: barramundi, catfish, goannas, wallabies and turtles.
facts: Kakadu's rock art tradition is one of the longest continuous ones in the world, and the Bininj and Mungguy custodians still know the stories behind many paintings.
X-ray paintings show what you learn by butchering the animal: which parts are eaten and how.
Kakadu was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1981 for both its nature and its culture.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph tagged PD-Art there, also released under GFDL by the photographer

artworks.title: Book of Kells, Chi Rho page (folio 34r)

madeIn.name: Iona Abbey (or Kells), Columban monastery
madeIn.region: Inner Hebrides, Scotland (or County Meath, Ireland)

artworks.medium: Ink and pigments on calf vellum
artworks.description: The Chi Rho page opens the account of Christ's birth in Matthew's Gospel: the Greek letters Chi, Rho and Iota, the abbreviation of 'Christ', fill the page with spirals, interlace, animals and tiny human figures. The Book of Kells, a Latin Gospel book made in a Columban monastery around 800, is the most elaborately decorated of the Insular manuscripts. It has been at Trinity College Dublin since the seventeenth century.
facts: The manuscript has 340 folios of calf vellum, each page about 33 by 25 cm, bound since 1953 in four volumes.
It contains ten full-page illustrations and was made in a Columban monastery in Ireland or Scotland around 800.
UNESCO added the Book of Kells to its Memory of the World Register in 2011.

credit.author: Unknown Columban scribes/illuminators, c. 800; reproduction uploader not stated (PD-Art)

contributed.note: Best colour reproduction of the Chi Rho page on Commons; only 1123 x 1558 px, below the 2000 px target. Every other Commons copy of fol. 34r is smaller (484 x 641 PNG) or a black-and-white lantern slide (KU Leuven GD017031, 3797 x 3230). A larger scan of a different full-page illumination (fol. 32v, 2202 x 2918, from Trinity College Dublin's digital collections) is listed as alternative 1. Trinity's own digital collection is not used because its image licence was not verified as free. Dates, size (33 x 25.5 cm), vellum and shelfmark from Wikidata Q204221 and en.wikipedia 'Book of Kells'; place of creation is uncertain (a Columban monastery in Ireland or Scotland), Iona chosen with coordinates from Wikidata Q610.

artworks.title: Eland, uKhahlamba-Drakensberg
artworks.medium: ochre, blood and egg binder on sandstone
artworks.description: An eland in shaded red and white on a sandstone shelter in the Drakensberg, painted by the San with a fine brush and a polychrome technique that modelled the animal's bulk. The eland is the animal that appears most often in San painting; it was the creature of greatest spiritual power, and the trance dance of the healers drew on its potency.
facts: The Drakensberg holds some 35,000 to 40,000 painted images in over 600 shelters.
Most of the paintings are less than 2,000 years old and some show horses and guns from the 1800s.
The park was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2000.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of the shelter wall

artworks.title: Travelers Among Mountains and Streams
artworks.movement: Northern Song monumental landscape (Northern Landscape style)
artworks.medium: Hanging scroll, ink and light colour on silk
artworks.description: A single cliff face rises almost the full height of the silk, with a thread of waterfall at its right and a mule train and travellers reduced to specks along the stream at its foot. Fan Kuan, a recluse who studied the mountains of Shaanxi directly, painted it around 1000; it is the defining work of Northern Song monumental landscape. The painter's signature, hidden among the foliage at lower right, was only rediscovered in 1958.
facts: Ink and light colour on silk, 206.3 by 103.3 cm, in the National Palace Museum, Taipei.
Fan Kuan's half-hidden signature in the leaves at the lower right was rediscovered in 1958.
The Ming painter-critic Dong Qichang is said to have called it the finest painting of the Song dynasty.

artworks.title: The Last Supper

location.name: Milan
location.institution: Refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie

artworks.medium: tempera on gesso, pitch and mastic
artworks.description: Painted on the north wall of the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, the mural shows the moment Jesus tells the apostles that one of them will betray him. Leonardo abandoned true fresco for an experimental tempera-on-dry-wall technique, which let him work slowly but began to deteriorate within decades.
facts: The apostles are arranged in four groups of three, reacting in waves to Jesus's announcement.
The perspective lines converge on Jesus's right temple.
A door was cut through the bottom of the mural in 1652, removing Jesus's feet.
The refectory survived an Allied bomb in 1943 that destroyed the roof and one wall; the mural had been sandbagged.

artworks.title: Plaque with Warrior and Attendants

madeIn.name: Benin City (royal court of the Kingdom of Benin)

location.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
location.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (Michael C. Rockefeller Wing)

artworks.medium: Cast brass (lost-wax)
artworks.description: A high-relief brass plaque from the royal palace of Benin showing a warrior chief in coral-bead regalia, flanked by two shield-bearing soldiers and smaller attendants, against a background incised with the river-leaf pattern. Plaques of this kind were cast by the royal brass guild around 1540–70 and nailed to the pillars of the palace. Benin's palace plaques and heads were seized by the British punitive expedition of 1897 and dispersed to museums and collectors; this one entered the Metropolitan Museum as a gift of Mr. and Mrs. Klaus G. Perls in 1990.
facts: Cast in brass by the lost-wax method by the Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n guild of the Oba's court, about 1540–70.
The British expedition of 1897 removed thousands of objects from Benin City; the British Museum alone acquired 203 plaques in 1898.
Height 47.6 cm, width 38.1 cm, depth 10.8 cm; the holes at the corners held the nails that fixed it to a palace pillar.

artworks.title: 1903 Wright Flyer

location.name: National Air and Space Museum, Washington, D.C.
location.institution: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

artworks.medium: Aircraft: spruce and ash airframe covered in muslin, cast-aluminium crankcase engine
artworks.description: The Wright Flyer is the biplane in which Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first sustained, controlled flights of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft at Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, on 17 December 1903. Built in the brothers' Dayton bicycle shop, it combined a wing-warping control system with a purpose-built 12-horsepower petrol engine and twin pusher propellers. This is the Smithsonian's laser scan of the original aircraft as it hangs in the National Air and Space Museum.
facts: Four flights were made on 17 December 1903; the longest covered 852 ft (260 m) in 59 seconds.
The 12-horsepower engine was built from scratch in six weeks by the Wrights' mechanic Charlie Taylor, with a cast-aluminium crankcase.
The Flyer joined the Smithsonian collection in 1948 after a long dispute between Orville Wright and the Institution over who flew first.

First-flight facts from Wikipedia 'Wright Flyer'.

artworks.title: Ford Model T Runabout
artworks.medium: steel body on wood frame, wooden spoke wheels
artworks.description: The car that put the world on wheels. Ford built more than fifteen million Model Ts between 1908 and 1927, and the moving assembly line at Highland Park cut the price from $780 in 1910 to $290 in 1924, when this two-seat runabout was the cheapest car in the catalogue. Simple, tough and endlessly adaptable, it was voted the most influential car of the twentieth century. This is an artist's reconstruction of the type, not a scan of a particular car.
facts: The assembly line cut the time to build a chassis from twelve and a half hours to ninety-three minutes.
"Any customer can have a car painted any colour that he wants, so long as it is black": from 1914 to 1925, black japan enamel was the only paint that dried fast enough for the line.
The engine ran on petrol, kerosene or ethanol, and farmers belted the rear wheel to saws, pumps and threshers.
Pedals, not a gear lever: the Model T's two-speed planetary transmission was worked with the feet.

contributed.note: Downloaded from Sketchfab by hand; artist-made model, not a scan

artworks.title: Bombe drums (Bletchley Park rebuild)

creators.name: Alan Turing
creators.role: designer (with Gordon Welchman's diagonal board; engineered by Harold Keen, British Tabulating Machine Company)

date.label: 1940 (original design; drums shown are a 1995–2008 rebuild)

location.name: The National Museum of Computing, Bletchley Park

artworks.medium: Electromechanical cipher-breaking machine component: Bakelite and metal rotor drum with 104 wire brushes
artworks.description: The bombe was the electromechanical machine with which Bletchley Park found the daily settings of German Enigma cipher machines. Designed by Alan Turing, refined by Gordon Welchman and engineered by Harold Keen at the British Tabulating Machine Company, each bombe carried 108 spinning drums, every drum wired to mimic one Enigma rotor. The drums shown here belong to the working reconstruction completed at Bletchley Park in 2008; the wartime machines were all broken up after the war.
facts: The first bombe, named 'Victory', was installed in Hut 1 at Bletchley Park on 18 March 1940.
Each bombe was about 7 ft wide, 6 ft 6 in tall and 2 ft deep, weighed about a ton, and had 108 positions for drums arranged in 36 triplets.
Each drum carried 104 wire brushes in four concentric circles of 26, giving two sets of input and output contacts on its mounting plate.

contributed.note: REPLICA: this shows drums on the working bombe rebuilt by John Harper's 'Phoenix' team of the BCS Computer Conservation Society (1994–2008), now at The National Museum of Computing on the Bletchley Park estate. All wartime bombes were dismantled after 1945 and no free photograph of a surviving original drum was found on Commons (Category:Bletchley Park Bombe has 62 files, all of the rebuild or wartime prints) or in the Science Museum Group collection; no 3D scan exists on Smithsonian, Met, SMG or Sketchfab. Chosen because it shows one Enigma-equivalent's three drums beside the bare mounting plates with their 104 contacts, which explains the mechanism; photographed 2011 at Bletchley Park. The physical size of a drum is not given by Wikipedia or the museum, so dimensions are null. Dates and mechanism facts from Wikipedia 'Bombe' (first bombe 'Victory' installed 18 March 1940; 108 drum positions; 104 brushes per drum; rebuild switched on 17 July 2008).

artworks.title: The first point-contact transistor (Bell Labs display)

creators.name: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain
creators.role: inventors (Bell Labs, under William Shockley's group)

madeIn.name: Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey

location.name: Nokia Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey

artworks.medium: Germanium point-contact transistor: germanium slab, gold-foil contacts on a plastic wedge, spring, Perspex mount
artworks.description: On 16 December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain of Bell Telephone Laboratories made a slab of germanium amplify an electrical signal by pressing two closely spaced gold contacts against its surface. Their point-contact transistor, demonstrated to Bell executives a week later, was the first working transistor and the ancestor of every semiconductor device since. The device shown is the display at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, generally identified as a replica of the original.
facts: The critical experiment on 16 December 1947 used a block of germanium with two very closely spaced gold contacts held against it by a spring.
Brattain made the two contacts by slitting a strip of gold foil wrapped over the point of a plastic triangle, leaving a gap of less than 0.1 mm.
The invention was demonstrated to Bell Labs management on 23 December 1947 and announced publicly in June 1948.

externalIds.commons-file: The First Transistor ever made, built in 1947 - Bell Labs.jpg

contributed.note: PROBABLY A REPLICA: the photo (Flickr 'Bell Labs 004', 2012) shows the point-contact transistor display at Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey; Commons titles it 'the first transistor ever made' and a second Commons photo of the same display (File:1st-Transistor.jpg, geotagged at Murray Hill) says 'original exhibited in Bell Laboratories', but the IEEE milestone page describes the Bell Labs Technology Showcase item as 'a replica of Bell Labs' first point-contact transistor' and Invention & Technology credits a 1997 Lucent replica, so treat it as a replica unless Nokia Bell Labs confirms otherwise; no free photo of a confirmed original was found, and no 3D scan exists (Smithsonian, Met, SMG, Sketchfab searched). The device is a germanium slab with two gold-foil contacts on a plastic wedge pressed by a spring, in a Perspex mount about the size of a hand; dimensions are not published by Wikipedia or Bell Labs, so null. Dates from Wikipedia 'Point-contact transistor' (first worked 16 December 1947, demonstrated 23 December 1947).

artworks.title: Apollo 11 Command Module Columbia

location.name: Washington, D.C.
location.institution: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

artworks.medium: aluminium honeycomb, stainless steel honeycomb, ablative heat shield
artworks.description: Columbia is the command module of Apollo 11, the first mission to land humans on the Moon, and the only part of that spacecraft to return to Earth. Michael Collins orbited the Moon alone in it while Armstrong and Aldrin were on the surface; all three rode it home through re-entry on 24 July 1969. The scan shows the exterior as it stands today, with the heat shield charred from re-entry.
facts: The crew wrote on the cabin walls during the flight, including a calendar Collins kept and the words "Spacecraft 107, alias Apollo 11, alias Columbia. The Best Ship to Come Down the Line. God Bless Her."
Collins named it after Jules Verne's cannon Columbiad and the ship Columbia Rediviva, the first American vessel to circle the globe.
After the flight it toured all fifty state capitals before coming to the Smithsonian in 1971.
The ablative heat shield reached about 2,800 °C during re-entry.

contributed.note: Initial import from Smithsonian 3D (exterior scan)

artworks.title: Cray-1 supercomputer
artworks.medium: Electronic computer: ECL integrated circuits on hand-wired modules in a Freon-cooled C-shaped cabinet
artworks.description: The Cray-1 was the first supercomputer built by Seymour Cray's Cray Research and the fastest computer in the world from 1976 to 1982. Its C-shaped tower kept every wire short, and the padded bench around the base hid the power supplies, while liquid Freon carried away the heat of its hand-wired logic. Eighty or more were sold to weapons laboratories, weather centres and universities; this one stands at EPFL in Lausanne.
facts: The first Cray-1 was installed at Los Alamos National Laboratory in 1976, after being announced in 1975.
It ran at an 80 MHz clock (12.5 ns cycle) with 64-bit words and vector registers, and contained over 60 miles of wire, no piece longer than three feet.
Over 80 Cray-1s of all types were sold at $5–8 million each, making Seymour Cray a celebrity and Cray Research a success.

contributed.note: No 3D scan of a real Cray-1 exists on the Smithsonian, Met, Science Museum Group or Sketchfab (the two Sketchfab Cray-1 models are artist-made, see alternatives), so a photograph is used. This is a Commons Quality Image: the complete machine, tower and padded power-supply bench, photographed in 2011 against a black background in the EPFL hallway in Lausanne; dual-licensed CeCILL / CC BY-SA 2.0 FR, attribution 'Photograph by Rama, Wikimedia Commons, Cc-by-sa-2.0-fr'. The serial number of the EPFL machine is not stated on Commons. Dimensions from Wikipedia 'Cray-1' infobox: height 196 cm, base diameter 263 cm, column diameter 145 cm, weight '5.5 tons' (Cray-1A; unit not specified, 4,990 kg if short tons). Date and sales figures from Wikipedia; 80 MHz clock from the Computer History Museum's Cray-1 exhibit page.

artworks.title: Apple Computer 1 (Apple I)

location.name: Washington, D.C.
location.institution: National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution

artworks.medium: Single-board microcomputer: printed circuit board with integrated circuits
materials: wood (base, as sold by some dealers)
artworks.description: The Apple Computer 1 is an 8-bit personal computer designed by Steve Wozniak and sold from July 1976 by the newly founded Apple Computer Company, with Steve Jobs handling the business side. Unlike most hobbyist computers of its day it was delivered as a fully assembled and tested circuit board, built around a MOS 6502 processor; the buyer still had to add a power supply, keyboard, cassette recorder and television. The board shown here is an artist's reconstruction of a complete Apple I set-up, including the optional wooden case and Apple-1 Operation Manual.
facts: Sold for $666.66; Wozniak chose the price because he liked repeating digits.
Only about 175 to 200 boards were made before the Apple II replaced it; production ended on 30 September 1977.
Ran a MOS 6502 processor at 1 MHz with 4 KB of RAM (expandable to 8 KB) and displayed 40 x 24 characters on a television.

artworks.title: Commodore 64

creators.name: Commodore International
creators.role: manufacturer (designed at its MOS Technology subsidiary)

artworks.medium: Home computer: moulded plastic case with integrated keyboard over a printed circuit board
artworks.description: The Commodore 64 is an 8-bit home computer introduced by Commodore International in January 1982 and sold from August of that year for US$595. Built around the MOS Technology 6510 processor with 64 KB of RAM, the VIC-II graphics chip and the SID sound chip, it undercut the Apple II, IBM PC and Atari machines and was sold in department and toy stores as well as computer dealers. This scan shows the original beige 'breadbin' case of 1982-84, before the slimmer C64C restyle.
facts: First shown at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas on 7-10 January 1982; marketed from August 1982 at US$595.
Guinness World Records lists it as the best-selling desktop computer model of all time, with estimates of 12.5 to 17 million units sold.
Its MOS 6510 CPU, VIC-II video chip and SID 6581 sound chip were all made by Commodore's own chip subsidiary MOS Technology; production ended with Commodore's bankruptcy in April 1994.

artworks.title: Apple IIc
artworks.medium: Personal computer with built-in keyboard and 5.25-inch floppy drive
artworks.description: The Apple IIc, introduced by Apple Computer in April 1984, packed a complete Apple IIe-compatible system, including a 5.25-inch floppy drive, into a compact housing with a fold-out carrying handle; the c stands for compact. It was the first product in Apple's Snow White design language, created with Hartmut Esslinger's frog design, and its off-white Fog colour and ribbed styling set the look of Apple hardware for the rest of the decade. The machine was usually sold with the matching 9-inch Monitor IIc shown here.
facts: Released on 24 April 1984 at Apple's 'Apple II Forever' event, priced at US$1,295.
Weighs 7.5 lb (3.4 kg) and runs a 65C02 at 1.023 MHz with 128 KB of RAM.
First Apple product in the Snow White design language by Hartmut Esslinger of frog design; discontinued in August 1988 in favour of the IIc Plus.

artworks.title: Rickroll
altTitles: Rick Astley - Never Gonna Give You Up (Official Video)
artworks.medium: music video, 3:33, shown as a silent three-second loop
artworks.description: The rickroll: a link that promises one thing and delivers Rick Astley's 1987 video for "Never Gonna Give You Up". It began on 4chan in May 2007 as a twist on an older duck-themed prank, spread through the whole internet within a year, and has never gone away. The video itself was shot in London by Simon West and became, through the prank, one of the most-watched clips on YouTube. Shown here at the size of a 110-inch screen, frozen until you come close.
facts: On 1 April 2008 YouTube rickrolled its own front page: every featured video linked to this one.
Rick Astley himself rickrolled the 2008 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, popping out of a float mid-song.
The video's YouTube id, dQw4w9WgXcQ, is recognised on sight by enough people that it is a meme in its own right.
The still and the loop are shown under fair use; the video and song remain the property of their owners.

artworks.title: iPhone (1st generation)

madeIn.name: Cupertino, California (designed; assembled by Foxconn in Shenzhen, China)

artworks.medium: Smartphone: aluminium and black polycarbonate body, 3.5-inch glass multi-touch display
artworks.description: Apple's first iPhone, unveiled by Steve Jobs at Macworld on 9 January 2007 and released that June, replaced the keypad of earlier phones with a 3.5-inch multi-touch screen and a single home button. Combining a phone, an iPod and an internet browser in one slab of aluminium and glass, it set the pattern that nearly every smartphone has followed since. This exhibit is a CC BY artist's model of the handset, not a scan of a particular example.
facts: Announced on 9 January 2007 and released in the United States on 29 June 2007 at $499 for the 4 GB model and $599 for 8 GB.
It measures 115 x 61 x 11.6 mm and weighs 135 g, with a 3.5-inch 320x480 display and 128 MB of memory.
About 6.1 million units were sold before it was discontinued on 11 July 2008 in favour of the iPhone 3G.
